title: The Vardic Holds
subtitle: From the Age of Oars to the Compact of Nine Anchors
summary: How a coast of fjords and quarrelling jarldoms became an industrial confederation that still measures people by what they have done.
content:
> *"Ask a Vard where they come from and they will name a Hold. Ask who they are and they will tell you what they have made."*
> — northern saying

The **Vardic Holds** are a loose confederation of northern Holds: jarldoms, industrial ports, island settlements, fortress-cities and the land around them. Their culture prizes craftsmanship, reputation, self-reliance, oaths, exploration, and above all leaving behind something worth remembering. A great engineer, a great shipwright, a warrior or an explorer can all earn the same standing, as long as what they did is worthy of a saga.

The Holds are now one of the great industrial powers of the north, but industry did not replace the old Vardic way of life. The Vards absorbed it. Old shipwright dynasties became engineering houses, and smithing traditions became industrial institutions. The maker's marks, knotwork, animal motifs, names and family symbols that once decorated weapons and longships moved naturally onto engines, firearms, tools, factories and ironclads.

This entry covers how the Holds came to be. Their religion is described in [[old-gods-of-the-holds|The Old Gods of the Holds]], and how they dress, build and mark their work in [[iron-timber-and-names|Iron, Timber, and Names]].

## A Coast That Resists Kings

The northern homeland is cut apart by fjords, islands, mountains, forests and cold seas. Travel between valleys is often easier by water than by land, and a settlement on one side of a mountain can have little reason to obey a ruler on the other.

Kings have united large parts of the north more than once. Their kingdoms rarely outlived a few generations. What endured was the **Hold**: a settlement, the territory around it, and the people attached to its ruler, traditionally a **Jarl**. Succession differs from Hold to Hold. Some jarls inherit their seat; others are elected, chosen by negotiation, or follow a custom particular to their Hold.

A Vard's first loyalty is still usually to a Hold, not to "the north" as a whole. That is less a failure of unity than a choice the Vards keep making.

## The Age of Oars

Long before the furnaces, the Vards were known abroad as sailors, merchants, explorers, mercenaries, raiders and shipwrights. Foreign chronicles tend to remember the raiding. The Vards remember something broader.

In the Age of Oars, prestige came from going somewhere unfamiliar and returning with something worth remembering: maps, wealth, foreign techniques, stories, trade routes, knowledge, new settlements, unusual materials. A voyage that brought back nothing was a voyage nobody sang about.

That old link between **exploration and reputation** never disappeared. It is a large part of why so many Vards have taken to the Gates with such enthusiasm.

## The Furnace Century

The industrial transformation of the Holds began with rich coal deposits and a rapidly expanding knowledge of metallurgy. Small forges grew into foundries. Foundries grew into industrial districts, shipyards and mining settlements. Harbours built for wooden ships learned to build iron ones.

Industry reinforced the old values instead of erasing them. Vardic machines frequently carry maker's marks, names, family symbols, decorative metalwork and engraved motifs. To a Vard, a machine with no mark of its maker can feel strangely anonymous, as if nobody were willing to stand behind it. Particularly impressive machines may even receive proper names.

### The Hrafneld

The **Hrafneld** was not necessarily the first steamship or the first armoured vessel built in the Holds. Its importance is cultural: it was the first modern industrial ship remembered as looking unmistakably *Vardic*. It had a long, low hull, an iron raven at its prow, engineering left proudly visible, and decorative metalwork drawn from the old northern ship traditions.

Its builder was the shipwright **Sigrun Veyrsdottir**, and the ship shaped Vardic warship design for generations.

> **At the launch of the Hrafneld, as the story is told**
>
> A foreign observer on the quay watched the iron raven slide into the water and said, loudly enough to be heard, "A barbarian longboat wrapped in iron."
>
> Sigrun Veyrsdottir did not look away from her ship.
>
> "Then perhaps you should avoid meeting it at sea."

Whether those were her exact words matters less than the fact that every Vard knows them. The exchange is part of the accepted story of the Hrafneld, and it captures something the Holds still believe: that something can look old and work very well indeed.

## The Wars of Smoke

The Furnace Century made the Holds rich, and wealth sharpened old rivalries. Powerful jarls and industrial interests began trying to dominate their neighbours. Foreign powers saw an opportunity and exploited the disputes to win mining concessions, shipping rights, political influence and favourable treaties.

The conflicts that followed are remembered together as the **Wars of Smoke**. They were devastating. Factories burned, harbours were blockaded, years of industrial work were destroyed, and some of the older Holds disappeared altogether.

The Wars of Smoke taught the north a hard lesson: each Hold on its own was vulnerable, both to its neighbours and to foreign interference.

## The Compact of Nine Anchors

The wars ended when nine powerful jarls agreed to negotiate at **Skeld Sound**. Tradition says the talks were held aboard ships anchored in neutral water, because none of the nine trusted the others enough to meet on land.

The agreement they reached, the **Compact of Nine Anchors**, rests on three principles:

- foreign powers may not seize recognised Vardic territory;
- each Hold keeps control of its own internal laws;
- when the north faces a common threat, every Hold is expected to provide ships, troops, supplies or other aid.

The Compact is the basis of the modern Vardic confederation, and its centre is weak on purpose. The Holds cooperate because cooperation is useful. They stay separate because independence is itself something they value.

> **A harbour negotiation, as northern sailors like to retell it**
>
> The Aurelian envoy laid out the plans: a deep-water harbour, modern cranes, a coaling station, all paid for by the Empire.
>
> Jarl Stenvar read every page. Then he asked one question.
>
> "Will your flag fly above the harbour?"
>
> The envoy hesitated. "Naturally."
>
> The jarl leaned back in his chair.
>
> "Then build it somewhere else."

## What You Have Done

Family matters in the Holds, and so do your Hold and your profession. But what someone has actually *done* can matter more than any of them.

A respected Vard may be introduced with an accomplishment that works almost like a title:

> *Yrsa Halvardsdottir, Chief Engineer of the Third Dock, Builder of the Skeld Turbines.*
>
> *Torren Vask, Breaker of the East Siege.*

Not every Vard carries such a title, and nobody gives themselves one. They belong to people whose deeds others agree are worth repeating.

This is one reason Endros draws so many Vards. The Gates are a place where a person can become famous quickly: through discovery, survival, engineering, exploration or something nobody has done before. A shipwright's apprentice can come home with a name.

## The Holds and the Gates

The Vardic instinct toward the impossible is practical:

> If something cannot yet be forged, tested, built with or understood, then the problem is temporary.

Vards are unusually comfortable treating supernatural materials as engineering challenges. That does not make every Vard reckless, and plenty of Vardic Expeditioners are careful to the point of superstition. But in the Holds, direct experimentation is far more acceptable than it is in [Verna](factions.html#verna) or the [Tianzhao Mandate](factions.html#tianzhao-mandate), where caution, classification and precedent come first.

> **Overheard in an assay room in Endros**
>
> The Vernan researcher had spent ten minutes on the sample's history: where it was found, who had handled it, what it did not react to.
>
> The Vardic engineer waited politely until she finished.
>
> "At what temperature does it melt?"
>
> "We don't know that it does."
>
> "Good. Then that's the first thing we'll find out."

The most famous story of this attitude belongs to the metallurgist **Edda Skorn**.

> **Edda Skorn and the indestructible fragment, as it is usually told**
>
> An early expedition into the Green Vault brought back a fragment of black, metallic material that seemed impossible to damage. The University of Verna proposed a long period of formal analysis.
>
> Edda Skorn asked for three days.
>
> She tried heat, acid, pressure and every practical test her workshop could offer. Nothing marked it. On the third day she set the fragment on her anvil and struck it with a hammer.
>
> The hammer broke.
>
> Edda looked at the pieces of her hammer, then at the untouched fragment, and said: "Excellent."

The fragment later became the subject of a joint Vardic–Vernan research effort, and what that research found has not been made public. The Vards do not tell the story for its ending. They tell it because failing to damage or understand the material did not discourage Edda Skorn. It made the problem worth her time.
